one_liner: Rust x86/x64 decoder, formatter, encoder and assembler; decodes 4-7x faster than Zydis, XED and bddisasm in disas-bench.
what_it_does: A complete x86 toolkit for 16/32/64-bit code: table-driven Decoder producing a 40-byte Instruction, formatters for masm, nasm, gas (AT&T) and Intel (XED) syntax, an encoder and BlockEncoder that re-encode instructions at a new address, a CodeAssembler (asm.mov(eax, edx)) and an instruction-info API (registers and memory read/written, RFLAGS, CPUID feature, control flow). The API is its own, not a Capstone/Zydis/XED look-alike: decoder.can_decode()/decode_out(&mut instr) and formatter.format(&instr, &mut String). Official bindings exist for .NET, Java, Python, JavaScript/WebAssembly and Lua; there is no C or C++ API.
how_it_is_fast: The decoder dispatches through 256-entry handler tables per opcode map (legacy, VEX, EVEX, XOP, MVEX), each entry a (decode fn pointer, handler data) pair, and reads operand bytes with unaligned pointer loads guarded by one bound check against a pointer capped at 15 bytes past the instruction start. decode_out writes into a caller-owned 40-byte struct, so nothing is allocated or returned by value. The benchmarked formatter is SpecializedFormatter<TraitOptions>, a masm-only formatter whose options are compile-time trait constants (db/dw/dd/dq support and output-capacity checks compiled out); the crate README says it is about 3.3x faster than the general formatters for decode+format.
when_to_use: Bulk disassembly of large x86-64 binaries (whole .text sections, crash-dump or JIT-code scanning) where the decoder is the bottleneck and the caller is Rust or one of the bindings.
Tools that need decode, re-encode and assemble in one library: moving or hooking code (BlockEncoder fixes up branches), patching, or emitting instructions with CodeAssembler.
Analysis passes that need per-instruction register, memory and flag effects or CPUID feature classes without a second library.
no_std or WebAssembly targets: the crate supports #![no_std] (with alloc) and ships an npm/WASM build; features can be trimmed (decoder only, one formatter).
when_not_to_use: Raw decode speed is the only criterion: the current upstream athre0z/disas-bench charts (October 2025, Ryzen 9 9950X and i9-13900K) show yaxpeax-x86 ahead of iced in both decode only (about 460 vs 360 MB/s and 405 vs 390 MB/s) and decode+format (about 198 vs 160 and 192 vs 166 MB/s); values read off the bars.
C or C++ projects that want a native API: there is none (open issues #728 'C/C++' and #775 'Support for C?'), so you need your own Rust FFI shim; Zydis, XED, bddisasm or diStorm link directly.
Non-x86 ISAs, or Intel APX: APX support is an open request (#626, October 2024).

You need formatted text in nasm, gas or Intel syntax at the benchmarked speed: the fast path is masm-style SpecializedFormatter only; the general formatters are about 3.3x slower per the crate README, which puts decode+format near 45 MB/s on the 2021 machine (derived estimate), below diStorm's 58.85.
You depend on frequent releases: the last crates.io release is 1.21.0 (2024-01-20); open issues #762 and #783 ask for a new one and master has seen mostly dependency bumps since.

integration.dependencies: lazy_static (serde optional); also published to NuGet, PyPI, npm and Maven
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.57 for crates.io 1.21.0 (rust_version in crates.io metadata); master's Cargo.toml says 1.64.0
integration.platforms: any Rust target, including no_std and wasm32; decodes x86 16/32/64-bit code only
integration.thread_safety: not documented; Decoder and formatter are per-use objects over borrowed input, so use one per thread

gotchas: Harness note (icedland/disas-bench, the 2021 numbers): the iced driver lets the decoder skip every byte of an invalid instruction and formats Code::INVALID entries, while the current upstream athre0z/disas-bench iced driver counts valid and bad instructions, re-syncs one byte after an invalid decode and skips formatting it; libraries therefore did not walk identical instruction streams in the 2021 run. The effect on a mostly valid xul.dll .text is probably small but was never quantified.

Also in that harness: the decode-only driver never reads the decoded Instruction, the C drivers time CPU time with clock() while the Rust drivers time wall clock in whole milliseconds, each configuration runs once, MB/s is really MiB/s, and iced is built from unpinned git master. The README's '>250 MB/s, >130 MB/s' claim links to disas-bench commit a865849, not the 2021-06-11 results commit.

Peak decode+format speed needs SpecializedFormatter with ENABLE_DB_DW_DD_DQ = false and the unsafe verify_output_has_enough_bytes_left() overridden to return false, plus LTO and codegen-units = 1 in your release profile, exactly as the crate README's 'Disassemble as fast as possible' section and the bench driver do. Its masm output is not guaranteed to re-assemble.

decode_out on bad bytes returns Code::INVALID and advances by the bytes consumed, not by one; resync yourself (as upstream's driver does) if you need byte-granular recovery. Open issue #828 reports a decoder/encoder length mismatch for redundant REX prefixes.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Over yaxpeax-x86 when you also need an encoder, assembler, instruction-info API, several output syntaxes or .NET/Python/JS/Java bindings; yaxpeax-x86 now edges it on raw decode in upstream disas-bench. Over diStorm3, Zydis, XED and bddisasm when you can call Rust: iced decodes 2-7x faster than all of them in both the 2021 and 2025 runs, but those four have native C APIs.
verified_claims_summary: In iced's own disas-bench fork (2021-06-11; i5-6600K, Kubuntu 21.04, gcc 10.3.0 with LTO for the C libraries, Rust 1.52.1 with LTO, Firefox 86 xul.dll 77 MB .text) iced decoded at 256.69 MB/s vs diStorm 92.17, Zydis (min) 61.33, XED 55.39, bddisasm 35.48 and Zydis 34.19, and decoded+formatted at 149.21 MB/s vs diStorm 58.85, Zydis 22.24, XED 15.67 and Capstone 14.02 (10.6x Capstone, derived). The upstream athre0z/disas-bench charts from October 2025 (Ryzen 9 9950X; i9-13900K) still put iced 2-7x ahead of every C library (decode+format about 160 MB/s vs Capstone 27 and Zydis 33 on the 9950X) but behind yaxpeax-x86.
status_note: Maintenance mode: MIT, 3.6k stars and about 3.5M crates.io downloads (1.1M recent), last release 1.21.0 on 2024-01-20, last non-bot merge 2026-06-13 and only dependency bumps since; stable and safe to depend on for x86 decoding, but no APX and no C API.
